There’s no cost to process the op in the implementation, but the balance change won’t run any EVM code, just deposit funds Sorry forgot to press reply but ^ gotcha, i guess im more referring to withdrawal credentials that are contracts that account for beaconchain balances and want stakers to prove their withdrawals before taking away balance from the contract. iguess thats not really an option with the current design? I’m not great on the contracts topic.. my understanding is they can accrue balance and have some kind of other interaction that would distribute that balance, and the fee occurs at that point… so small deposits add up, and when it’s worth it they get distributed…. There was a point made about a type of address that only runs code and can’t handle having balance, but I’m not sure about all the finer points of that discussion… I guess the other important thing CL side was the change to eth1 address is a 1 shot deal, so if you choose the wrong address, there’s no fixing that, and the user needs to get it right … The problem raises its head when there is a single contract that is the target for multiple validators, and wants some way of distributing the rewards. This would likely require some form of proof that a given amount of ETH was transferred to the contract from a given validator, and if the amount of ETH was very small then the gas to prove the transfer could eat up a fair chunk of the rewards. There are alternatives, such as having a separate contract for each validator, but that burns a chunk of gas in creating them as well as losing out on some more interesting options for contracts with pooling and the like. blocks will contain the changes, so it could be calculated per validator id, not sure if that makes life easier... it'd literally have validator id and balance change and it could be computed fairly easily, but it's another process yep, the problem is that the proof of the withdrawal against the block header could actually end up being a significant fraction of the rewards haha i wouldnt suggest doing that in evm, otherwise yes -but someone will figure out an efficient process now that the rules are known... I guess on the flip side you don't want the EVM spending its life running 'free' contracts either The issue here is what the EVM has access to. I tend to agree with <@144468805697929216> here but I haven't seen anyone from the community actually complaining about this so it makes me think that no one is making proofs on chain. You can cheaply make proofs on the beacon chain once you have the state root on the evm

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
The problem raises its head when there is a single contract that is the target for multiple validators, and wants some way of distributing the rewards.  This would likely require some form of proof that a given amount of ETH was transferred to the contract from a given validator, and if the amount of ETH was very small then the gas to prove the transfer could eat up a fair chunk of the rewards.

There are alternatives, such as having a separate contract for each validator, but that burns a chunk of gas in creating them as well as losing out on some more interesting options for contracts with pooling and the like.
